title: SSH vs Telnet: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Telnet is a postcard, and anyone can read it. S S H is a locked box. Always use the locked box.

scenes.heading: Postcard vs lockbox
scenes.narration: Both reach the device, but one is safe. Telnet uses port twenty three and sends everything in plain text. S S H uses port twenty two and encrypts the whole session. To turn S S H on, you need a hostname, a domain and an R S A key. Then limit the V T Y lines to S S H only.

scenes.heading: Enable SSH
scenes.narration: Here's the quick recipe. Set a domain name. Generate the R S A keys. Open the V T Y lines. Allow S S H only.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three traps. Both use T C P, only S S H encrypts. S S H isn't on until you make keys. The transport command goes under the V T Y lines.

items.wrong: Telnet is safer because it uses TCP
items.right: Both use TCP; only SSH encrypts

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. S S H is encrypted, and Telnet is not. Generate R S A keys to turn S S H on. Allow only S S H on the V T Y lines. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva SSH lab.
